'PROCLAIM GABRIELA NOW'

Members of the women’s group Gabriela held a protest at the Commission on Elections (Comelec) head office in Intramuros, Manila, on Wednesday, September 3, to call for the immediate proclamation of the Gabriela Women’s Party in Congress.

With the cancellation of Duterte Youth party-list’s registration, they argued that there is no longer a legal barrier to Gabriela’s proclamation. As the next qualifying party-list group, they said Gabriela should be proclaimed without further delay.

In the 2025 midterm elections, Duterte Youth received 2,338,564 votes and was entitled to three seats in the House of Representatives, while Gabriela placed 55th in the party-list race with 256,811 votes.

📷: The STAR/Edd Gumban

Related: https://t.co/wvNYorWg1j

data.text:
Metro Manila once again faced heavy flooding this Habagat season. In a recent episode, PGMN anchor Orion Perez Dumdum explained that the capital’s flooding problem has been recurring for centuries and was already documented as early as the Spanish colonial period.

Orion cited records from Spanish authorities and Jesuit scientists in the 1800s, which identified several districts in Manila as vulnerable to severe floods. 

Areas such as Sampaloc, Binondo, Santa Cruz, Quiapo, Malate, Ermita, and Arroceros were marked as unsafe for permanent settlement due to recurring inundations. 

Parts of Marikina Valley, along with floodplains in Cainta, Taytay, and Pasig, were also recognized as danger zones and were historically used as rice fields because of their naturally waterlogged conditions.

He noted that these early warnings were later reflected in urban development plans, including Daniel Burnham’s 1905 Manila Plan and the World Bank–funded Metroplan of 1977 led by architect and urban planner Felino Palafox Jr. Despite the proposals, Orion said most long-term flood control measures were not carried out, leaving Metro Manila vulnerable to recurring disasters.

Drawing a comparison with Singapore, Orion pointed out how the city-state once faced similar flooding but invested heavily in prevention. 

The government built deep and wide canals, expanded esteros, and reinforced waterways to divert heavy rainfall toward reservoirs and the sea. 

These investments, he said, reduced the city’s flooding incidents even though Singapore receives more annual rainfall than Metro Manila.

In contrast, Orion explained, flood management in the Philippine capital has been undermined by rapid population growth and unregulated settlements. 

Many waterways have been blocked by informal housing, while some residential subdivisions were built on former rice fields and floodplains, areas historically prone to inundation.

Orion also highlighted governance as a major obstacle. With 17 local government units operating independently in Metro Manila, he said coordination on flood control projects has been slow and often inconsistent.

 The absence of a central metropolitan authority, Orion added, has caused delays and conflicts in the approval of large-scale infrastructure.

“Hindi natin masosolusyunan ang problema ng pagbaha kung hindi natin babaguhin ang ating bulok na sistema,” Orion said, emphasizing that structural reforms are necessary.

He warned that without long-term planning and continuity, projects such as the dredging of Laguna de Bay or the construction of spillways will remain unfinished, leaving Metro Manila exposed to the same cycle of floods year after year.
